Cycling in Phoenix

South Mountain at dawn, the McDowell loops, the Greenbelt

Getting around. The rules.

Phoenix is a winter cycling town: the riding runs from November to April, summer highs average 104 to 106 F, and the rides go out at first light. The climb is South Mountain’s Summit Road, closed to cars on Sunday mornings. The long loops go around the McDowell Mountains through Scottsdale, Rio Verde and Fountain Hills, and over Usery Pass along the Salt River in the East Valley. The easy day is the 11-mile Indian Bend Wash path through Scottsdale. The riding sits 6 to 25 miles out of downtown in every direction, so you will want a car. American checks a packed bike as a standard bag (Oct 2026); one south Scottsdale shop rents a carbon road bike at $90 a day (Oct 2026); no Valley shop says in writing that it receives a shipped bike. Bring yours for anything longer than a day.

Best months
November to April. Summer highs average 104 to 106 F. On Extreme Heat Warning days the city closes named preserve trails from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; in 2026 those closures began March 19. From May to October, ride at first light and carry all your water.
Nearest airport
Phoenix Sky Harbor International (PHX), 4 mi

Clubs and collectives in Phoenix

  1. Phoenix Metro Bicycle Club

    No-dropBeginner friendly

    The Valley’s big road club. Saturday Cycling (Saturdays, 7:30 am) from Kiwanis Park in Tempe is, in the club’s words, the big weekly ride for everyone: no-drop with a sweep, about 25 or 35 miles, beginners and newcomers welcome. The club also runs the Granada Park breakfast ride (Sundays, 6:30 am) in Phoenix and a no-drop ride (Wednesdays, 7:30 am) that moves around the Southeast Valley. Visitors are always welcome; helmet on, no earphones.

    In the directory: Saturday Cycling (Saturdays, 7:30 am) →

  2. Scottsdale Cycling

    The fast crowd at Gainey Village, Scottsdale Rd and Doubletree Ranch Rd. The two Gainey rides (Tue and Thu, 5:30 am) are rated advanced and start in the dark most of the year, so bring front and rear lights. The Fuss Buss (Saturdays, 6:00 am) is four to five hours and more relaxed, but still a drop ride, and it ends at coffee. The Strava club is set to invite-only: ask to join there, and expect rain to cancel the ride.

    In the directory: Gainey Thursday (Thursdays, 5:30 am) →

  3. McDowell Mountain Cycles

    No-dropGravelWomen / trans / femme

    The Fountain Hills shop posts a ride for every kind of bike on its monthly calendar. There is a no-drop road ride (Some Saturdays, 6:30 am) of 30-plus miles from the shop, and Sunday Funday (Some Sundays, 6:30 am), about 40 no-drop miles of gravel, road and singletrack. TNR (Tuesdays, 7:00 pm), 15 to 20 miles of night mountain biking, and the Ladies Mountain Bike Ride (Some Mondays, 7:00 am) both leave the Four Peaks lot in McDowell Mountain Regional Park. The shop says everyone is welcome and to check its Facebook page for times.

    In the directory: MMC Saturday Road Ride (Some Saturdays, 6:30 am) →

  4. Valley Epic Rides

    The weeknight mountain bike group on Meetup: Taco Tuesday (Tuesdays, 6:30 pm) on South Mountain’s trails and the Night Rider series (Wednesdays, 6:30 pm) on Trail 100 in the Phoenix Mountains Preserve, 7 to 12 miles in about two hours. Lights are a must. The group asks you to have five or so mountain bike rides behind you, and points very new riders to the beginner-friendly weekend rides it posts now and then. Join the group and RSVP; a ride with no sign-ups six hours out may be cancelled, and summer rides cancel for heat and dust storms.

    In the directory: Taco Tuesday Ride at South Mountain (Tuesdays, 6:30 pm) →

  5. Bike Saviours Bicycle Collective

    The volunteer-run co-op at 420 S Perry Lane, Tempe: an open shop with tools and volunteers who teach, plus repurposed bikes and parts. Open shop Saturday and Sunday noon to 6, Wednesday and Thursday 3 to 9; Monday is donations only, Tuesday and Friday closed (Oct 2026); 602-429-9369. The shop posts a safe-space agreement and says it will always say no to racism, sexism, ageism and homophobia.

  6. Black Girls Do Bike: Phoenix

    BIPOCWomen / trans / femme

    The Phoenix chapter of the national group, which says it centers women of color in cycling. The chapter runs through its Facebook group (facebook.com/groups/BlackGirlsDoBikePhoenix), where rides are posted; join the group and ask for the next one. No ride schedule is published on the site.

How Phoenix rides: the zones, getting here

About Phoenix

Downtown Phoenix is the center for every distance on these pages, and the riding is at the edges of the Valley. This guide names its zones: South Mountain and Ahwatukee on the south edge; Scottsdale and the northeast (Gainey Village, the Indian Bend Wash greenbelt, Fountain Hills, Rio Verde and McDowell Mountain Regional Park); the East Valley (Tempe, Mesa, Usery Pass and the Salt River, Chandler); and the dirt (Trail 100 in the Phoenix Mountains Preserve, the Competitive Track at McDowell Mountain Regional Park, South Mountain’s trails). Every listing says which one it sits in and how far it is from downtown.

Phoenix is Cycle for Change’s home base. one·n·ten, the LGBTQ youth organization in Phoenix, is one of the orgs Cycle for Change rides for. Its Cycling 4 one·n·ten ride is Saturday, November 7, 2026, 20 or 62 miles from Prisma Community Care on Central Ave, and Robert is riding it. The 2027 edition is on the 2027 calendar for November. The rest of the winter calendar: the Valley of the Sun Stage Race in February, Belgian Waffle Ride Arizona on March 7, 2027 and the Cactus Cup at McDowell Mountain in March, and the HonorHealth Tour de Scottsdale on April 10, 2027.

Riding in Phoenix

The ride for the evening you land is the Indian Bend Wash path: 11 miles of concrete path through Scottsdale’s greenbelt, with more than 24 underpasses and bridges at the big streets. The climb is South Mountain’s Summit Road, 7 miles and about 1,330 feet from the ranger station to the towers. The city closes it to cars for Silent Sunday (Sundays, 5:00 am), a closed road rather than a led ride. The long loop goes around the McDowell Mountains from the Safeway at DC Ranch, up Pima to Dynamite, over to Rio Verde and down Saguaro to Shea. 50 miles and about 2,750 feet, with no water on the route page. The East Valley’s loop is Usery Pass and the Salt River out of Mesa, 27 miles and about 1,500 feet, with the only water at the top of Usery. Dirt is Trail 100 across the Phoenix Mountains Preserve and the Competitive Track at McDowell Mountain Regional Park, where the Four Peaks lot has water, showers and a bike wash.

The group rides are the way in. Scottsdale Cycling leaves Gainey Village, the southeast corner of Scottsdale Rd and Doubletree Ranch Rd, for two fast weekday rides (Tue and Thu, 5:30 am) and the Fuss Buss (Saturdays, 6:00 am). They start in the dark most of the year, so bring lights. TriScottsdale rolls from Village Tavern on the same block for its long weekend ride (Saturdays, 6:30 am). Phoenix Metro Bicycle Club’s Saturday Cycling (Saturdays, 7:30 am) from Kiwanis Park in Tempe is no-drop with a sweep, the easiest group ride in the Valley for a visitor. Its Granada Park ride (Sundays, 6:30 am) ends at breakfast. Regroup’s coffee ride (Saturdays, 6:30 am) leaves the café in Tempe and comes back to it. McDowell Mountain Cycles in Fountain Hills posts a no-drop road ride (Some Saturdays, 6:30 am) and Sunday Funday gravel (Some Sundays, 6:30 am). On dirt, Valley Epic Rides meets for Taco Tuesday (Tuesdays, 6:30 pm) on South Mountain and the Night Rider series (Wednesdays, 6:30 pm) on Trail 100. The Downtempo ride (Mondays, 8:00 pm) is the slow, no-drop social ride from Civic Space Park downtown.

Getting to Phoenix

Fly into Phoenix Sky Harbor (PHX), about 4 miles east of downtown. American and Southwest use Terminal 4; Alaska, Delta, United, Frontier, JetBlue and the rest use Terminal 3 (the airport’s airline list, Oct 2026). The free PHX Sky Train runs 24 hours from both terminals to the Rental Car Center, where 14 companies rent, and to the Valley Metro Rail stop at 44th and Washington streets. Reserve a car, because walk-up cars are limited. You will want one: the shops in this guide run from 2 to 23 miles out of downtown, and the riding zones sit further apart than that. Rideshare picks up at marked curbs at Terminals 3 and 4, and a taxi to downtown Phoenix is a $20 flat rate (Oct 2026). The Bring-your-bike page has American’s bike rules, the rental math and the shipping gap.

Questions about riding in Phoenix

Should I bring my bike to Phoenix?

Yes, for anything longer than a day. American checks a cased bike as a standard bag, $45 each way paid online when it is your only checked bag (Oct 2026). The one shop that publishes a rental price, Bike Emporium in south Scottsdale, charges $90 a day for a carbon road bike (Oct 2026), so renting only wins on a single day. No Valley shop says on its own site that it receives a shipped bike; call before you send one. Bring your gravel bike too: the one gravel rental with a published spec is a 7-speed.

When is the riding season in Phoenix?

November to April. Summer highs average 104 to 106 F, and on Extreme Heat Warning days the city closes named preserve trails from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; in 2026 those closures began on March 19. If you come between May and October, ride at first light, carry all your water, and know that the weeknight dirt rides cancel for heat and dust storms.

Where do the group rides start in Phoenix?

Scottsdale Cycling leaves Gainey Village, the southeast corner of Scottsdale Rd and Doubletree Ranch Rd, for two fast weekday rides (Tue and Thu, 5:30 am) and the Fuss Buss (Saturdays, 6:00 am); TriScottsdale leaves Village Tavern on the same block for its long weekend ride (Saturdays, 6:30 am). Phoenix Metro Bicycle Club’s no-drop Saturday Cycling (Saturdays, 7:30 am) leaves Kiwanis Park in Tempe, and Regroup’s coffee ride (Saturdays, 6:30 am) leaves the café at 1205 N Scottsdale Rd in Tempe. McDowell Mountain Cycles in Fountain Hills posts a road ride (Some Saturdays, 6:30 am) and Sunday Funday gravel (Some Sundays, 6:30 am) from the shop, and Global Bikes’ Chandler North ride (Saturdays, 6:00 am) leaves its Ray Road store. Every ride near Phoenix, with its day and time, is in the rides directory.

Can I rent a road or gravel bike in Phoenix?

Bike Emporium in south Scottsdale publishes its fleet: a carbon Cannondale SuperSix EVO with Shimano 105 in sizes 48 to 61 cm at $90 per 24 hours, a Marin Kentfield 1 aluminum gravel bike at $60 and a Cannondale Habit full-suspension mountain bike at $85, with a helmet, lock and bottle cage on every rental and pedals and a repair kit on the road and mountain bikes, not stated for the gravel bike (Oct 2026). It is closed Sundays. McDowell Mountain Cycles in Fountain Hills rents road, gravel, mountain and e-bikes with no prices on its site and delivers to McDowell Mountain Regional Park. Bike Barn in Phoenix rents road and mountain bikes through a booking page, and Airpark Bike Co in Scottsdale rents mountain bikes if you bring a hitch rack.

Do I need a car to ride in Phoenix?

Yes. The riding sits 6 to 25 miles out of downtown in every direction: Granada Park about 6 miles north, Regroup in Tempe about 8 east, Gainey Village about 11 northeast, Global Bikes in Chandler about 14 southeast and Fountain Hills about 23. From Sky Harbor the free PHX Sky Train runs 24 hours to the Rental Car Center, where 14 companies rent; reserve ahead, because walk-up cars are limited. A taxi to downtown is a $20 flat rate (Oct 2026).

When is South Mountain’s Summit Road closed to cars?

Every Sunday the city stops cars at the 1.0 mile marker from 5 to 10 a.m., and on the 4th Sunday of the month the road is closed to cars all day, 5 a.m. to 7 p.m., with drivers parking at the Activity Complex (City of Phoenix). It is a closed road, not a led ride. The park’s entrance and parking hours are 5 a.m. to 7 p.m., and the climb from the ranger station to the towers is 7 miles and about 1,330 feet.
